ingredients.name: guanciale
ingredients.original: 150 g guanciale, cut into thick strips

ingredients.name: coarse salt
ingredients.original: 1 tbsp coarse salt, for the pasta water

steps.text: Fry the guanciale in a dry pan until the fat renders and the edges turn crisp. Take the pan off the heat.
Whisk the yolks, whole egg, most of the pecorino and the pepper into a thick paste.
Boil the spaghetti in salted water until just al dente. Save 2 dl of the pasta water.
Toss the drained pasta in the pan with the guanciale and its fat. Let it cool for a minute.
Add the egg mixture off the heat and toss hard, adding pasta water a splash at a time until the sauce is creamy. Serve with the rest of the pecorino.
steps.critical: Do it off the heat; above about 70 °C the eggs scramble.

notes.techniques: The sauce is an emulsion of rendered pork fat, starchy pasta water and egg. It is built off the heat by tossing constantly.
notes.chemistry: Egg yolk proteins thicken from about 65 °C and curdle above about 70 °C, so the residual heat of the pasta is enough. Starch from the pasta water stabilises the emulsion.
notes.spiceProfile: Only black pepper, used generously. Salty, sharp pecorino and sweet pork fat carry the flavour.
notes.variations: This is the Roman standard: guanciale, pecorino and mostly yolks, with no cream, garlic or onion.

ingredients.name: coarse salt
ingredients.original: 1 tbsp coarse salt, for the pasta water

steps.text: Cook the pancetta and garlic in the oil until the pancetta is golden. Discard the garlic.
Beat the eggs with the parmesan and pepper.
Boil the spaghetti in salted water until al dente. Save 2 dl of the pasta water.
Off the heat, toss the pasta with the pancetta, then the egg mixture, loosening with pasta water until glossy.
steps.critical: Keep the pan off the heat or the whole eggs set into scrambled egg.

notes.techniques: Same off-heat emulsion as the Roman version, but whole eggs give a looser, less rich sauce.
notes.chemistry: Egg white sets at a lower temperature than yolk (about 62 °C), so whole-egg sauces scramble more easily. Work quickly and use pasta water to cool and loosen.
notes.spiceProfile: Milder and nuttier than the Roman version: parmesan is less salty and tangy than pecorino.
notes.variations: Uses easier-to-find pancetta, parmesan and whole eggs, plus a hint of garlic. The result is lighter and milder than the guanciale-pecorino classic.

ingredients.name: smoked bacon
ingredients.original: 150 g smoked bacon, cut into strips

ingredients.name: coarse salt
ingredients.original: 1 tbsp coarse salt, for the pasta water

steps.text: Fry the bacon until crisp, then add the onion and cook until soft.
Whisk the cream, yolks, parmesan and pepper together.
Boil the spaghetti in salted water until al dente. Save 1 dl of the pasta water.
Add the pasta to the bacon pan, pour in the cream mixture and toss over low heat until it just thickens. Loosen with pasta water and top with parsley.
steps.critical: Only warm it until the sauce coats the pasta; boiling splits the yolks.

notes.techniques: Cream dilutes the yolks, so the sauce can sit over low heat briefly without curdling.
notes.chemistry: Fat and water in the cream raise the temperature at which the egg proteins coagulate, giving a wider safety margin.
notes.spiceProfile: Smoky bacon and onion make it sweeter and rounder than the Italian versions.
notes.variations: A common non-Italian take: smoked bacon, onion and cream make a forgiving, saucier dish. Purists do not use cream.
